input: Given question: A 12-year-old boy has injured himself playing football and has been given some ibuprofen to help relieve some of the pain. Which domain is inhibited on the Prostaglandin H Synthase enzyme and how does this drug work? Option A: A) Cyclo-oxygenase domainB) Irreversible non-competitive inhibitor Option B: A) Peroxidase domain B) Reversible competitive inhibitor Option C: A) Cyclo-oxygenase domain B) Reversible competitive inhibitor Option D: A) Peroxidase domain B) Irreversible non-competitive inhibitor The correct answer is Option C.
reference: COX domain inhibited - this is where arachidonic acid and O2 form a complex which is then cleaved by the peroxidase domain to produce PGG2, which is a prostaglandin H synthase intermediate. PGHS only produces PGE2 therefore PGGS is produced instead. Since PGGS cannot form GMP, it is instead converted into PGE2 via the peroxidase domain which is not inhibited. Ibuprofen works as a competitive inhibitor by outcompeting the substrate, arachidonic acid, for the active site of PGSH. It mimics the role of arachidonic acid and therefore prevents the formation of PGG2. Since PGGS cannot be produced, neither PGE2 nor PGGS can be formed. Therefore there is less PGE2 present, which is the prostaglandin involved with platelet aggregation, leading to slower rates of haemostasis, explaining why NSAIDs are able to reduce fever.
best_explanation:
Explanation: The drug ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that works by inhibiting the activity of the Prostaglandin H Synthase enzyme. This enzyme is responsible for the production of prostaglandins, which are involved in the inflammatory response. By inhibiting this enzyme, ibuprofen reduces the production of prostaglandins and therefore reduces pain and inflammation.

The domain that is inhibited on the Prostaglandin H Synthase enzyme by ibuprofen is the cyclo-oxygenase domain. This is the domain that is responsible for the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins. Ibuprofen is a reversible competitive inhibitor of this domain, meaning that it binds to the enzyme and blocks its activity, but the binding site is not irreversibly occupied. This allows the enzyme to continue to function when the drug is not present.

In summary, ibuprofen works by inhibiting the cyclo-oxygenase domain of the Prostaglandin H Synthase enzyme, which is responsible for the production of prostaglandins. This reduces inflammation and pain.

Option A: Faecal calprotectin Option B: Anti-tTG antibodies Option C: Anti-TPO antibodies Option D: Endoscopy Option E: Anti-gliadin antibodies The correct answer is Option B.
reference: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibodies (tTG) are found in coeliac disease. (They cross the intestinal mucosa and are found in the blood.) Calprotectin is released by the inflammated intestine into faeces as a protective measure to prevent the absorption of bacteria and their components. It is not specific to coeliac disease. Gliadin is a component of gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. Anti-gliadin antibodies are found in both coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis. Anti-TPO antibodies are made against the peroxidase part of thyroid hormones. (coeliac disease is associated with a lack of thyroid hormones.) (B12, iron, calcium and folate). The symptoms described in the given input such as weight loss, bloating, and abdominal pain, along with the physical examination finding of dermatitis herpetiformis, suggest the presence of coeliac disease. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a common symptom of coeliac disease, which is an autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation and damage to the small intestine.

input: Given question: A 4g-6g dose of paracetamol is a toxic dose and greater than 12g is a lethal dose.  In the event, that patient overdoses on paracetamol, which of the following would be a suitable treatment to manage the patient? Option A: Cytochrome P450 enzymes Option B: Hepatic glutathione Option C: n-acetylcysteine (NAC) Option D: n-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPBQI) Option E: UGT enzymes The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Drug metabolism occurs in order to deactivate the drug and also to make it water soluble for excretion. Phase 1 of metabolism involves different reactions (such as oxidation, reduction, isomerisation) depending on the drug and type of enzyme involved, but it is essentially a precursor to phase 2. Phase 1 metabolites may create reactive intermediate compounds eg ramipril to ramiprilat (antihypertensive) and in this case paracetamol to NAPBQI. Important phase 1 enzyme include cytochrome P450 and are on demand enzymes through the pregnane-x receptor mechanism. There are multiple types of isoforms of CYPs and UGTs for different substrates.  Phase 2 involves acting upon phase 1 metabolite, deactivating it and making it water-soluble (can involve replacing the drug's pharmacophoric region with sugar or a sulphate group). Glucuronosyl Transferases (UGT) is phase 2 and they combine the phase 1 metabolites with glucuronic acid (UDP) deactivating the metabolite and making it water-soluble (in Gilbert's and Crigler-Najjar syndrome, there is a mutation to a gene which results in the absence of UGT enzymes required to conjugate bilirubin).  In paracetamol, the majority of this drug bypasses phase 1 and undergoes phase 2 of metabolism. Some of this drug, however, does undergo phase 1 metabolism, producing the toxic metabolite of NAPBQI which is deactivated by binding to hepatic glutathione.  If a dose of paracetamol is exceedingly large, the hepatic glutathione stores become depleted and  UGT enzymes become saturated and hence there is build up of toxic NAPBQI which can damage hepatocytes. N-acetyl cysteine can be infused and this tops up the depleted levels of hepatic glutathione.  It's worthwhile appreciating enzyme kinetics, that Vmax is the concentration of the drug at which an enzyme is at a maximum turn over rate. Km is Vmax/2.

If there is a toxic amount of paracetamol in the body, then glutathione, an antioxidant, will be depleted.  N-acetylcysteine (NAC) can be given as an antidote for paracetamol overdose.  NAPBQI is the toxic compound produced from paracetamol metabolism.  UGT enzymes are involved in the glucuronidation of paracetamol, which renders it water soluble for excretion.  A less serious overdose can be treated with UGT enzymes to increase excretion of paracetamol.  A lethal dose of paracetamol will deplete glutathione and NAC will not be able to reverse the toxic effects.  Treatment will then be supportive, e.g. glutathione supplements may be given if paracetamol is not treated with NAC.  It is important to treat with NAC within 8 hours of ingestion of paracetamol.  Any later and liver damage may be irreversible.  It is also important to be aware of the amount of paracetamol in a person and to seek medical attention if a large quantity has been taken. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A certain medical student has an unhealthy obsession with killer whales and whilst watching Free Willy becomes extremely emotional. They begin to cry uncontrollably. What nerve is causing this? Option A: Lacrimal nerve, a branch of CN V1 Option B: Frontal nerve, a branch of CN V1 Option C: Pterygopalatine nerve, a branch of CN V2 Option D: CN III Option E: Greater petrosal nerve, a branch of CN VII The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Tearing is caused by the lacrimal nerve (a branch of CN V1) but the emotions that trigger this are sensory impulses from the frontal nerve (also a branch of CN V1). Whilst watching the film and becoming emotional, the frontal nerve is stimulated and sends sensory impulses to the brain which recognises the emotion and triggers the lacrimal nerve, resulting in tears being produced. However the greater petrosal nerve is responsible for the actual act of crying as it causes the muscles of the face to contract and produce sound. This student should probably seek help... or at least stop watching sad films. Refer to "The Orbit, Eye, Ear and Thyroid Gland" lecture from Case 14. Useful resources:http://www.anatomystuff.co.uk/repository/product/user/img_img_9781587799259_dissection_guide_eye_chart.jpghttp://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimal_nerve#cite_note-Gray's_Anatomy.jpg[edit] CryingA diagram showing the nerves involved in crying is available at http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Tears_of_emotion.svg/300px-Tears_of_emotion.svg.png (This is a Wikipedia file, so is probably accurate...)The greater petrosal nerve is actually a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not VII as I mistakenly wrote in the question. Also, the lacrimal nerve is a branch of CN V1, not V2. My apologies for any confusion caused. For more information, see "The Orbit, Eye, Ear and Thyroid Gland" lecture from Case 14 and the links provided above. --Joe Wilson 15:04, 16 April 2014 (UTC)
best_explanation: The correct answer is Option E: Greater petrosal nerve, a branch of CN VII. The emotional response of the medical student is likely caused by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates the body's response to stress. The greater petrosal nerve, a branch of CN VII, plays a key role in the HPA axis by conveying sensory information from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland. This nerve is responsible for the regulation of the body's stress response, and its activation can lead to an emotional response, such as crying. input: Given question: A patient comes into clinic complaining of an inability to move their wrist resulting in a 'wrist drop'. Option A: Median Nerve Option B: Ulnar Nerve Option C: Radial Nerve Option D: Musculocutaneous Nerve Option E: Medial pectoral nerve The correct answer is Option C.
reference: The answer is C - radial nerveThe radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the arm (and therefore the wrist) and is the terminal branch of the posterior chord of the brachial plexus - which is damaged in 'wrist drop'A - the median nerve supplies the flexor muscles of the forearm and handB - the ulnar nerve supplies the medial side of the forearmD - the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior armE - the medial pectoral nerve does exist (it innervates the medial side of the chest wall) but it isn't involved in wrist drop This was covered in the upper limb lecture in PCS 3Weeks 4-7: General Surgery (Mr Andrew Shore)Week 4: Introduction to surgical specialitiesWeek 5: OrthopaedicsWeek 6: Plastic and reconstructive surgeryWeek 7: Burns and wound careThese are all really interesting and I found them quite useful to get an overview of the different surgical specialties. I would recommend looking up 'osteotomy' on Wikipedia - it's where they cut a bone and then hold it in place with plates and screws (really cool!)I found the plastic and reconstructive surgery lecture particularly interesting - I had no idea that people could do so much with just tissue! I would highly recommend the documentary 'The Secret Life of Chaos' if you get the chance to watch it - it's not medical related but it's all about the science of randomness and it's amazing!xWeeks 8-10: Psychiatry (Dr Alice Fabbian)Week 8: Introduction to psychiatryWeek 9: Neurophysiology and neuropharmacologyWeek 10: Psychological therapies and counsellingI found these lectures really interesting and it's made me think more about how different illnesses can affect people in different ways. best_explanation: Damage to the radial nerve results in a 'wrist drop' in which the patient is unable to lift the wrist. There is also likely to be a loss of sensation in the lateral aspect of the forearm. This is because the radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the arm and the lateral aspect of the forearm. The radial nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the hand, the thumb and the index and middle fingers. As the thumb, index finger and middle finger are mobile the radial nerve is most likely to be damaged in a 'wrist drop'. reference: In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), there is a failure to produce steroid hormones by the adrenal gland. This most commonly involves the combined inability to synthesize sufficient cortisol (glucocorticoids) and aldosterone (mineralocorticoids). Secondary adrenal insufficiency may result from impaired stimulation or production of adrenal steroid hormones due to defects in the hypothalamus, pituitary gland or adrenal gland (e.g. Sheehan's syndrome). Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency caused by insufficient circulating cortisol; it is usually caused by pituitary tumours or long-term use of glucocorticoid medication. Adrenal crisis is characterized by hyperglycemia, electrolyte imbalances (low K+, high Na+), and acidosis. It may also present with non-specific complaints such as nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Adrenal crisis typically occurs when a person is already immunocompromised (for example, by HIV or cancer), malnourished, or suffering from severe infection. Management of the adrenal crisis typically involves administering large doses of glucocorticoids (such as hydrocortisone) and, often, fludrocortisone acetate (a synthetic mineralocorticoide). Patients in adrenal crisis may also receive intravenous saline solution to correct dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. Sodium levels are generally normal or only slightly elevated in Addison's disease. Potassium levels are generally elevated. Hormone levels in Addison's disease: low aldosterone, low cortisol, low catecholamines (low/normal ACTH). Immune suppression (such as that caused by AIDS) or malnutrition can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency. ACTH and CRH stimulate the adrenal glands to release cortisol and aldosterone, respectively. If these hormones are not produced, or if the body does not respond to them, the result is adrenal insufficiency. input: Given question: After surgery a patient is left with a hoarse throat when she speaks. This is due to damage of a branch of one of the following nerves. Which is it ? The other nerves do not have any branches which go to the larynx, so they are all incorrect. For more information, the intrinsic muscles of the larynx are the cricothyroid, stylohyoid, thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid. These muscles are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which is a branch of the vagus nerve (the other two branches of the vagus nerve are the sino-atrial node and the aortic arch). The extrinsic muscles of the larynx are the sternothyroid, omohyoid, and thyrohyoid. These are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (which is also called the twelfth cranial nerve). The nerve which innervates the intrinsic muscles of the pharynx is the glossopharyngeal, and the extrinsic muscles there are the palatoglossus, palatopharyngeus, and tonsillar capsule. The nerve which innervates the extrinsic muscles of the oropharynx is the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. reference:

The heart has a resting rate of 60 beats per minute. Therefore, in one minute there will be 60 beats. In a 3 minute period there will be 180 beats. To find the proportion of time spent between the higher (systolic) and lower (diastolic) numbers, you do 180 beats / 3 minutes x 60 beats = 1 : 3 The proportion is therefore 1/3 For more information refer to the NHS website: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/contraception-guide/how-do-contraceptives-work/page-2/How to calculate your blood pressure http://www.heart.org/HEARTORG/Conditions/HighBloodPressure/AboutHighBloodPressure/How-to-calculate-your-blood-pressure_UCM_301784_Article.jsp#.WVNK7IvyuUk

input: Given question: During the first 8 weeks of pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblastic cells of the placenta produce human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). What hormone does hCG mimic in order to maintain the corpus luteum? Option A: Luteinising hormone Option B: Follicle stimulating hormone Option C: Gonadotropin releasing hormone Option D: estrogen Option E: progesterone The correct answer is Option A.
reference: During the first 8 weeks of pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblastic cells of the placenta produce hCG. This hormone mimics LH and therefore prevents the regression of the corpus luteum, which would normally occur at 8 weeks resulting in menses. This ensures that progesterone levels remain high enough to maintain the endometrial lining of the uterus, until the embryonic pole is capable of doing so (at around 6 weeks). If the corpus luteum were to degenerate, progesterone levels would decrease, resulting in the degeneration of the endometrium and menstruation. Reference: case 7- hormonal control of menstruation lecture. Question 3:What are the physiological changes that occur in a woman's body during menstruation? Answer:Progesterone and oestrogen decrease, leading to the degeneration of the endometrium. The corpus luteum degenerates and therefore, progesterone levels fall. The lack of progesterone leads to the contraction of the myometrium, causing the sloughing of the endometrium and menstruation. Also, FSH increases to thicken the uterine lining before ovulation. During the follicular phase, FSH causes the conversion of steroids (from the stromal cells of the theca externa) into oestrogen by the stromal cells of the follicle.During the luteal phase, FSH cause the conversion of steroids (from the corpus luteum) into progesterone by the stromal cells of the theca interna.  Menstrual bleeding lasts on average 5 days but can vary between 3-7 days. During the menstrual phase, the released eggs (ova) are picked up by the fallopian tube and transported to the sigma opening where fertilisation may occur. A mucus plug seals off the cervix and the internal os is closed by the low pH and high viscosity of the mucus.  Progesterone and oestrogen increase, leading to thickening of the uterine lining. FSH also increases, thickening the uterine lining before ovulation. The thickened lining of the uterus is essential for implantation. Oestrogen converts to progesterone to create a suitable environment for the newly formed blastocyst to implant into the uterine lining. Growth hormone also increases, increasing the number of spiral arteries in the lining of the uterus, thus increasing blood flow to the uterus. Question 4:What are the physiological differences between the menstrual cycles of adolescent girls and adult women?Answer:Adolescent girls have irregular menstrual cycles due to variable secretion of sex hormones. Their pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus is not consistent, leading to irregular secretion of LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary. As a result, their patterns of oestrogen and progesterone secretion from the ovaries are irregular. Adult women have more regular menstrual cycles because the pattern of GnRH release has been established and is more consistent. The pattern of LH and FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary is more regular, which means that the pattern of oestrogen and progesterone secretion from the ovaries is more regular. In adult women, the interval between menstrual cycles is called the menstrual cycle length and is usually between 21 days and 35 days in duration. Whereas, in adolescent girls, the interval between menstrual cycles is called the menstrual cycle variability and is often between 21 days and 40 days in duration. Furthermore, adolescent girls have higher levels of plasma oestrogen than adult women during the mid-luteal phase (after ovulation) and this is thought to be why they experience more pronounced physical and behavioural changes associated with the oestrogen rise. Adult women experience a smaller rise in oestrogen during the mid-luteal phase due to lower plasma levels of oestrogen relative to progesterone. This explains why adult women experience less pronounced physical and behavioural changes associated with the oestrogen rise.  Source: Reproductive hormones and menstrual cycles lecture Case 8 + tutorial PCS2 Tutorial Booklet - see how it relates to your own menstrual cycles!  Question 5:What is the role of progesterone

Option A: Luteinising hormone is the hormone that hCG mimics in order to maintain the corpus luteum during the first 8 weeks of pregnancy. The syncytiotrophoblastic cells of the placenta produce hCG during this time, which helps to maintain the corpus luteum by mimicking the action of luteinising hormone (LH). This helps to maintain the levels of progesterone, which is essential for the development of the placenta and the growth of the embryo.

Explanation:
During the first 8 weeks of pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblastic cells of the placenta produce human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). hCG is a hormone that plays a crucial role in maintaining the corpus luteum, which is an important endocrine gland that plays a vital role in pregnancy.

The corpus luteum is responsible for producing progesterone, which is a hormone that plays a crucial role in preparing the uterus for pregnancy and maintaining the pregnancy. Progesterone also helps to regulate the menstrual cycle and prevent ovulation.

The function of hCG is to mimic the action of luteinising hormone (LH) in the body. LH is a hormone that is produced by the pituitary gland and plays a crucial role in the regulation of the menstrual cycle and the production of progesterone.

During pregnancy, hCG produced by the syncytiotrophoblastic cells of the placenta helps to maintain the levels of progesterone in the body, which is essential for the development of the placenta and the growth of the embryo.

In summary, the hormone that hCG mimics in order to maintain the corpus luteum during the first 8 weeks of pregnancy is Luteinising hormone (LH). This helps to maintain the levels of progesterone, which is essential for the development of the placenta and the growth of the embryo.

input: Given question: Jude, 23, has recently been diagnosed with a respiratory condition. Spirometry results from investigations shows residual volume is increased as he is able to inspire more air than he expires. From this alone, which of the following is it probable that Jude may have? Option A: A restrictive lung disease Option B: An obstructive lung disease Option C: Kyphoscoliosis Option D: Muscle weakness Option E: Tense ascites The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
1) In obstructive lung disease, air remains in the lungs after normal expiration. This is due to blockages in the airways or an increase in airway resistance. 2) People with obstructive lung diseases are unable to exhale completely. Thus, the total amount of air remaining in the lungs (residual volume) is greater than normal because they cannot get rid of all the air they inspired. 3) Residual volume is measured using spirometry and is defined as the maximum amount of air that a person can still exhale after normal exhalation. 4) A normal value for residual volume is around 1 litre. Values greater than 1 litre indicate an increased residual volume and suggest an obstructive lung disease. A) Restrictive lung disease is where lung expansion is limited, so the volume of air in the lungs is reduced. This means that people with restrictive lung disease cannot inspire enough air. Therefore, they would not be able to expire all of the air they have inspired, so residual volume would not be increased. B) Correct! C) Kyphoscoliosis is a medical condition where there is a curving of the spine into an "S" or "C" shape. D) Muscle weakness can be caused by many things, but wouldn't affect residual volume as it is related to airways being blocked or having increased airway resistance. E) Tense ascites is when abdominal swelling occurs due to an excessive build-up of fluid in the abdomen. This doesn't relate to the lungs and would not cause an increased residual volume. In restrictive lung disease, lung expansion is limited, so the volume of air in the lungs is reduced. This means that people with restrictive lung disease cannot inspire enough air. Therefore, they would not be able to expire all of the air they have inspired, so residual volume would not be increased. input: Given question: Martha is suffering from the early stages of heart failure whereby her heart is beginning to be less effective but her neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms mean that she has few symptoms. At a routine check up, her GP notices that her resting heart rate has increased since her last check up, which the GP puts down to this compensatory response. Which of the following neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms is responsible for this increase? Option A: Endothelin pathway activation Option B: Left ventricular hypertrophy Option C: Parasympathetic inhibition Option D: RAAS activation Option E: Sympathetic stimulation The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The sympathetic nervous system is activated. This acts to increase heart rate and contractility in order to increase cardiac output and blood pressure. However, this increases the workload and oxygen demand of the heart which can cause decompensation if it worsens the left ventricular dysfunction. A (endothelin pathway activation) - This increases blood pressure by vasoconstrictionB (left ventricular hypertrophy) - This increases the mass of the muscle making up the left ventricleC (parasympathetic inhibition) - Not a direct neurohormonal response to heart failureD (RAAS activation) - This increases blood pressure by salt and water retention and other methodsE (sympathetic stimulation) - CORRECT The compensatory responses to heart failure increase the workload of the heart, leading to decompensation, which causes a spiral of heart failure. This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘CARDIAC FAILURE: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY, PRESENTATION & INVESTIGATION’.
best_explanation: In heart failure, the sympathetic nervous system is activated as the body tries to compensate for the reduced pumping efficiency of the heart. This increases resting heart rate, and also increases contractility and conduction in the AV node (therefore increasing the heart's pacemaker activity). Endothelin pathway activation - this is an alternative spelling of endothelial pathway activation, and either is acceptable. This is a pathway whereby endothelin 1 is released in response to increased ventricular end diastolic volume, which causes vasoconstriction in order to increase blood pressure. Left ventricular hypertrophy - this is where the ventricular wall thickens, which might be due to hypertension, or in the case of heart failure, is a response to increased pressure being asked of the heart. Parasympathetic inhibition - in response to increased demands on the heart, the parasympathetic nervous system will inhibit activities such as digestion, in order to divert blood to the heart. RAAS activation - this is activated when there is evidence of fluid overload, in order to increase water and salt reabsorption from the kidney, therefore increasing fluid and salt output.  Sympathetic stimulation - as the heart pumps less effectively, less blood is circulating in the body and therefore less reaches the brain. This triggers a sympathetic response to increase heart rate and contractility in order to increase cardiac output. There is no visible pattern to the waves.The ventricles are still conducting normally but the atria are no longer able to contribute to ventricular filling and do not contract and relax in coordination with the ventricles. This means that blood begins to accumulate in the atria and begins to get pushed into the passages between the atria and ventricles (the PR intervals gets longer). The atria eventually become enlarged and can no longer maintain their normal role in blood cooling, filtering and initiation of circulation. Ischaemia may occur in the hand and fingers causing them to feel cold. There may also be a feeling of a 'thump' in the neck when the atria contraction finally ends and the atria walls return to their normal position. It is likely that the patient will experience palpitations and fatigue. answer C: this describes atrial fibrillation. reference: At the end of the second trimester, the foetus has an open blood supply via the placenta. The three shuttles (ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus) are kept open by the pressure in the pulmonary vessels being higher than the systemic vessels. At birth, the foramen ovale is a flap-like structure in the heart that allows oxygen-poor blood from the right atrium to flow to the left atrium. When the first breath is taken, oxygen enters the alveoli for the first time, which signals the arterioles to dilate. This sudden dilation leads to a large drop in pressure in the pulmonary system, and the pressure in the right atrium becomes significantly lower than in the left atrium. As a result, the flap-like structure called foramen ovale closes, preventing oxygen-poor blood from flowing to the left atrium. This is the mechanism by which oxygen-poor blood is prevented from mixing with oxygen-rich blood in the left atrium, ensuring that the baby's circulatory system functions properly.

input: Given question: What is the main difference between Macrophages and Dendritic Cells? Option A: Dendritic cells are located in peripheral tissues, whereas macrophages are only found in the blood. reference: Dendritic cells are very similar to macrophages in many ways and have some overlapping functions. Both cells are capable of recognising and internalising pathogens and secreting inflammatory cytokines. However, dendritic cells have the additional ability to migrate from the site of infection via the lymphatic vessels to the draining lymph nodes where they can present T naïve T cells with MHC/peptide complexes. This allows the immune response to be initiated before any pathogen has reached the lymph node. reference: Strontium is a metal that has a chemical similarity to calcium. It is taken up by osteoblasts and reduced by osteoclasts, thus reducing bone resorption. This results in an increase in bone density and a decrease in the risk of bone fractures. Bisphosphonates, Raloxifene, and Teriparatide are also drugs that are used to treat conditions related to bone health, but they work in different ways and have different mechanisms of action.

input: Given question: Whilst managing a patient with AKI they begin to develop symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, altered mental state and asterixis. Elevated levels of what substance can these findings be attributed to? Option A: Creatinine Option B: Urea Option C: Potassium Option D: Lactic acid Option E: Calcium The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Answer = B - urea AKI related hyperureaemia is caused by increased blood concentration of urea due to decreased renal function. Urea is the end product of protein catabolism and is normally excreted by the kidney in the urine. When the kidneys are not able to remove urea from the blood at a normal rate, blood urea concentration increases. This is commonly caused by conditions that affect renal blood flow or glomerular capillaries. Treatment depends on the underlying cause but often includes fluid management and correcting electrolyte imbalances. A) creatinine is also a waste product generated from muscle metabolism and is normally excreted by the kidneys, however this is not the best answer as it is not as directly linked to the cause of AKI B) correct! as urea is the main component of urine C) potassium is also excreted by the kidneys in the urine and elevated levels are linked to AKI, however it is not as directly linked to the symptoms listed above D) lactic acid is not usually associated with AKI and is more commonly associated with liver/heart failureE) calcium is not really associated with AKI and is not likely to be measured in a patients serum as it isn't particularly indicative of anything relevant to AKI. For more information refer to Case 10 Acute Renal Failure lecture and SBA questions. PCS Unit 3 Renal & Hepatic Drugs Therapy (Case 10) 24/11/2016
==============================================================================================================================

This was covered in the Case 10 renal failure lecture. The key points were:A) creatinine is waste product generated from muscle metabolism and is normally excreted by the kidneys. However if kidney function deteriorates then creatinine will accumulate in the blood. This is used as a marker for how well the kidneys are functioning.B) In AKI there is hyperfiltration which puts strain on the glomerulus, this can lead to hematuria (blood in urine), increased levels of proteins not effectively filtered (e.g. albumin). C) in chronic renal failure concentrations of ions such as potassium, phosphate and acid can become abnormally high or low. D) urea is the end product of protein catabolism and is normally excreted by the kidney in the urine. If kidney function deteriorates then urea will accumulate in the blood. This causes the symptoms listed in the question. The increased urea degrades the plasma proteins and therefore leads to a negative nitrogen balance. It also stimulates the nervous system which causes the symptoms listed. E) Soft tissue calcification (e.g. of the heart) occurs in advanced chronic renal failure. This is due to the build up of calcium ions in the blood as the kidneys cannot excrete them properly. The exact mechanism causing this is unknown. From PCS unit 3 renal and hepatic drugs therapy case 10. I hope this helps and I haven't miss anything out! Let me know if you have any questions.

reference:
Adenosine - Class 5 – potent blocker of I(K,Ca) in myocyte – can be pro-arrhythmic in patients with long QT syndrome or Wolff Parkinson White. Amiodarone - class 3 – may have both pro-arrhythmic and anti-arrhythmic effects depending on dose and individual. Digoxin - class 1 - works as a negative phosphorylator in the sodium-potassium ATPase pump in cardiac myocytes, making it harder to depolarise. This increases the risk of TdP. Metoprolol - class 1 - a beta-blocker. Beta-blockers are part of the treatment for AF, but they can have pro-arrhythmogenic effects, especially if there is heart failure involved. They also lower the heart rate, which raises the stakes for any arrhythmia. Verapamil - class 4 – a calcium channel blocker – use in SVT, AVNRT, WPW. May increase the risk of TdP through its actions. B - Beta- lactams prevent the production of new bacterial walls by binding to penicillin-binding-proteins (PMPs), preventing cross linkages being formed between peptides in the wall. input: Given question: You are working in a GP surgery and speak to a father who is concerned about his 3 year old daughter. He says that she gets very out of breath just going up the stairs, is often tired and sleepy and sometimes says that her chest "feels funny". You agree to listen to her heart and think that you can hear a heart murmur. After further tests you explain to the father that you suspect that his daughter has a small hole in her heart due to the failure of an embryonic structure between the two atria to close. What is the name of this embryonic structure? Option A: Fossa ovalis. Option B: Ductus arteriosus. Option C: Left umbilical vein. Option D: Foramen ovale. Option E: Left auricle. The correct answer is Option D.
reference: A - Fossa ovalis is the feature on the wall of the inside of the right atrium of the heart which is left as a remnant of the closing of the foramen ovale. The fossa ovalis is present in a normally developed, healthy heart. B - The ductus arteriosus is the blood vessel in the developing foetus that connects the trunk of the pulmonary artery to the proximal descending aorta. It allows most of the blood from the right ventricle to bypass the non-functioning lungs. It is closes around the time of birth, and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.  C - The left umbilical vein is present during foetal development and carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the growing foetus. D - The foramen ovale is a small hole located in the septum of foetal hearts between the left and right atria. It allows passage of blood between the two atria (bypassing the ventricles) as there of no need for blood to be sent to the non-functioning lungs. It is one of two two foetal cardiac shunts, the other being the ductus arteriosus. The foramen ovale closes up around birth, leaving the fossa ovale which can be seen on the interior wall of the right atrium. E - The left auricle (names because of its ear shape) is a flap of muscle on the wall of the left atrium that is involved in pumping blood within the heart.  A hole in the heart, or Atrial Septal Defect is a congenital condition that often happens due to the failure of the embryonic structure - the foramen ovale - to close during early infancy. The condition can often be mild with no symptoms or complications, however if the ASD is severe it can cause damage to the lungs and overworking of the right side of the heart. In this case, the child is experiencing substantial symptoms, and so you may want to refer them to a cardiac specialist who may suggest surgical intervention to repair the hole.

input: Given question: You visit a patient with heart failure at his home as he hasn't attended any of his appointments for several weeks despite previous engaging with health care providers. When you arrive, you find that he is lying in his bed with 4  pillows and has dyspnoea even at rest. According to the New York Heart Failure Classification, which of the following is most appropriate? Option A: Class I Option B: Class II Option C: Class III Option D: Class IV Option E: Class V The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
ClassificationNYHFCSeverityI - No symptoms/minimal symptoms at restII - Dyspnoea at restIII - Dyspnoea on minimal exerciseIV - Dyspnoea at moderate exerciseV - Dyspnoea at maximal exerciseVI - Dyspnoea at everyday activities VII - Orthopnoea VIII - PNDX - X-ray evidence of pulmonary oedema (puffy lungs)IX - CMP- cardiac cachexia (wasting)X - HF hospitalisation XV - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation XVI - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation + ART (artificial lung support) XVII - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation + ART + defibrillator XVIII - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation + ART + defibrillator + ICD (implantable cardioverter-defibrillator) XIX - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation + ART + defibrillator + ICD + LVAD (left ventricular assist device) XX - PNDX + CMP + HF hospitalisation + ART + defibrillator + ICD + LVAD + OMT (cardiac transplantation) Treatment guidelines suggest that as soon as Phase I is reached (dyspnoea at rest), an LVAD should be inserted. This would mean that this particular patient should have an LVAD fitted immediately as he is already at phase IV (dyspnoea at moderate exercise). Other things to note from the NYHFC are that there is no mention of Class 0 (no symptoms at all) and that Class VI (dyspnoea at everyday activities) is equivalent to the "exertional" part of the FCRT.SOURCE: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9E; "Heart failure classification and prognosis" - page 872; ISBN: 978-1-5990-25onoan-recommended-reading-for-hf-module-2016-2017
Health Care Providers (HCPs) should be aware of the following when classifying a patient with heart failure:The NYHFC only goes up to Class IV - there is no Class 0 or Class I (as there is no symptomatology at all)Class I is equivalent to the FCRT's "at rest"Class II is equivalent to the FCRT's "at rest with oedema"Class III is equivalent to the FCRT's "with minimal activity"Class IV is equivalent to the FCRT's "on minimal exercise"Class V (and above) are not part of the FCRTIf a patient is classified as having dyspnoea at rest, then they should be given an LVAD immediately according to treatment guidelines (as they are already at phase IV - dyspnoea at moderate exercise)SOURCE: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9E; "Heart failure classification and prognosis" - page 872; ISBN: 978-1-5990-25onoan-recommended-reading-for-hf-module-2016-2017
In terms of treatment, NOTHING should be done to try and reverse heart failure (as this is often fatal) instead we should focus on treating the symptoms and trying to slow the progression of the condition. Some of the main drugs used are ACE inhibitors, Angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta blockers, diuretics and digitalis. In very severe cases, a cardiac transplant may be considered. It is important to remember that the aim of drug treatment is NOT to return the patient to normal life but to stabilise them at their current level of function.SOURCE: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9E; "Heart failure treatment" - page 872; ISBN: 978-1-5990-25onoan-recommended-reading-for-hf-module-2016-2017

Both however result in reduced EF and can lead to heart failure. With cardiomyopathy the heart muscle is simply weaker hence ejection fraction is lower
